question: A 2-year-old boy presents with fever (38.4°C), ear tugging, and irritability for 18 hours. Otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous right tympanic membrane without perforation. He has had one prior AOM episode. He appears well and is feeding normally. Which management plan is most appropriate?

answers.text: Watchful waiting with safety-netting for 48–72 hours; prescribe analgesia only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Watchful waiting is an option for mild AOM in children ≥2 years who are not severely ill, but this child is 2 years old with a bulging tympanic membrane — the AAP criteria allow watchful waiting here. However, the preferred approach when the tympanic membrane is clearly bulging is to treat. More importantly, if antibiotics are started, the correct dose is critical.

answers.text: Amoxicillin at standard dose 40–50 mg/kg/day for 5 days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard-dose amoxicillin is INCORRECT for AOM. Because Streptococcus pneumoniae strains with intermediate penicillin resistance require high drug concentrations in the middle-ear fluid, amoxicillin must be given at 80–90 mg/kg/day in two divided doses to achieve adequate bactericidal levels.

answers.text: Amoxicillin at high dose 80–90 mg/kg/day in two divided doses for 10 days

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. High-dose amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day) is the first-line antibiotic for AOM. The higher dose overcomes pneumococcal penicillin resistance in the middle-ear fluid. Duration is 10 days for children under 2 years or those with severe disease; 5–7 days may suffice for mild AOM in older children.

Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate) is reserved as second-line therapy when the child has failed high-dose amoxicillin, typically after 48–72 hours without improvement or when beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae is suspected. It is not the first-line choice for uncomplicated AOM.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the single most critical dosing rule in AOM is high-dose amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day. Standard doses (40–50 mg/kg/day) are insufficient to overcome pneumococcal penicillin resistance.

Well done. High-dose amoxicillin (80–90 mg/kg/day) is the cornerstone of AOM antibiotic therapy because pneumococcal resistance requires higher middle-ear drug concentrations than standard dosing provides.
